label: doc_title
text: WORLD OF SPORT.

label: paragraph_title
text: FOOTBALL

label: text
text: MISTAKES MADE BY RULING BODI

label: text
text: We have somehow grown to regard Cricket as a game conservative and even aristocratic, and Association football as the most democratic of sports, writes E. G. L. in All Sports. But these words, so freely used, are political terms. They refer to the governing spirit of the sport, not to the people who play it and watch it. And in this light can we describe football as democratic.

label: text
text: Jack Sharp used to be a professional gricketer; he has reverted to his amateur status, and is actually captain of Launcashire. The same might, conceivably, happen to Jack Hobbs. But if Charles Buchan wished to return to his amateur status and finish his football life with Loyton, or Binks, of Huddersfield, desired to give up professionalism and lend South Bank again, do you think he could? This apart from the club's consent.

label: text
text: Would the Football Association situation it? It is highly improbable. Indeed, we have only to turn to the report of the last meeting of the committee dealing with reinstatement to discover that the difficulty of persuading these gentlemen that it is not undesirable is enormous.

label: text
text: The same committee, it may be observed, also refused permission to severall old professionals to "sit on the Committee of Management" of such clubs as Tinotype Football Club, Bass Football Club (Burton-on-Trenton), and to one to act as a director of Accrington Stanley Football Club.

label: text
text: They think, apparently, that such a procedure would not be in the best interests of the game. Will they please tell us why? To us, the uninitiated public, who believe that some clients managers have more power and influence in football than some directors, it seems odd that an old player may be the former, but on no account the latter.

label: paragraph_title
text: CAN IT BE?

label: text
text:
Is it the idea that a professional should not be allowed to contribute to the good of football unless he accepts payment for it? How odd!
The M.C.C. take some hard knocks for their pains and principles, but we remember that their committee for choosing the teams to play South Africa in the Tests here last summer had instructions to consult a professional, as well as the team captain, if they deemed it necessary, and that, in fact, Hobbs was consulted.

label: paragraph_title
text: MISTAKEN POLICY

label: text
text:
Have the Football Association Selection Committee ever consulted anybody beyond their own little coterie? Possibly some of them have—an officially and rather in the nature of "sounding" opinion. But would have ever admit it?
So recently is when Vivian Woodward, an amateur, was good enough to lead England, and, later, when Arthur Grimsdell, a professional, stood out as the player and captain of the year in all four first-class intelligence and experience invited to express an opinion as to the players they were to lead on to the field? Oh, no.

label: text
text: We begin to find, now, that football is not so democratic as we had always thought. Indeed, a closer examination than this short article permits would reveal that the Football Association is something like a hierarchy, and as conservative a ruling body as there is in sport or elsewhere.

label: paragraph_title
text: VERY HOLEY

label: text
text:
In fact, when football comes to be called democratic we find so many holes in it, and such big ones, that while we are finding one we stumble into another.
Taking it broad and large, the weak spots with the strong, the Football Association is undeniably efficient defensively. Very little escapes its net of surveillance. But when we see an old player denied the privilege of working for the common weal of football for nothing, simply because he was once paid for playing, it seems absurd to attach the tag "democratic" to the gentry of Russell Square.

label: text
text: The outstanding features of our tour," said Mr. A.E. R. Gilligan, the captain of the M.O.O. team; in a talk broadcast to all stations from "2LO" "were the magnificent batting of Jack Hobbs and Herbert Satcliffe, the fine bowling of Maurice Tate," Strulwick's wicket-keeping, and the grand, all-round fielding of the team.

label: text
text: He paid a further tribute to Hobbs, who, he said, "is still the world's greatest batsman." Sutcliffe, he added, would without doubt be Hobbs's successor. Sutcliffe's three consecutive centuries, one in the first match at Sydney and two at Melbourne—will stand for all time.

label: text
text: Strudwick, as the wicket, showed the finest form of his whole career, and his keeping made all the difference in the world to Tate's bowling—"our only bowler," who took thirty-eight wickets in the series, beating Arthur Muiley's 36 wicket record in the 1921-22 Tests. Having stated that the fielding of his side was admittedly infinitely superior to that of the Australians, Mr. Gilligan recalled "Patsey" Hendren's magnificent work in the second match, when he must have saved two hundred runs.

label: text
text:
A "BARHACKER'S" GIFT:
'The much discussed habit of
"burracking" Mr. Gilligan's described us, humorous, insists nature, and meant to be, taken that way, but, if a player allowed himself to tie "ruttled" by it, the crowd was after him at once. Indeed, one Adelaide "barracker" was pleased with the way the visitors played their cricket and took the "barracking" that he made a gift of a travelling rug to Mr. Gilligan to keep him warm on his return to England.

label: text
text: Speaking of the 8-ball over, Mr. Gilligan thought it tended to slow the game up considerably. In Australia, he said, "wickets are just a batsman's paradise, and the bowler's life is not a happy one. Therefore, why handicap the bowler still further by making him do extra work each over? From a batsman's and fielder's point of view I don't think the game is seriously affected at all."

label: text
text: There was no doubt, however, that before the next M.C.C. team went to Australia, the matter would have to be thoroughly gone into by the governing bodies in both countries, as would also the question of the toss.

label: text
text:
A ROYAL WELCOME.
Mr. Gilligan paid a tribute to the hospitality extended to them in Australia, and referred to the kindness of the Governor-General (Lord Forster), who never missed a single ball bowled throughout the five Test matches, which lasted thirty-one days altogether. Thanks were due to the captain of the Maloja on the voyage home, who was Captain Shipley Warner, a

label: text
text: "When we arrived at Port Sudan," said Mr. Gilligan, "the Duke and Duchess of York came aboard after their four months' tour in Africa. The M.C.C. team had the great honour of being introduced to their Royal Highlyness, who were perfectly sweet and charming to us all. I regarded this not only as the very greatest compliment to the M.C.C. team, but also as the greatest honour that could have been, paid to cricket." After a compliment to Mr. F. C. Toone, their manager, Mr. Gilligan concluded by saving it was only a matter of time when an M.C.C. side recovered the "Ashes," and all were looking forward to the Australian visit next summer, when he hoped "Herby" Collins will be in charge.

label: text
text: DE LEON WINS AGAIN.

label: text
text: Gavino De Leon, now labelled "the Filipino Terror," scored another victory in Sydney on April 25, when he knocked out Jack Green. Green weighed nine stone and De Leon 8.1L.

label: text
text: Green had a lead at half wry. He hit the Filipino with all sorts of punches, but could not stop him getting to close quarters, where De Leon scored heavily to the body. De Leon forced the pace in the eleventh and fought like a tornado in the twelfth, when Green was so plainly beaten that the towel came in.

label: text
text:
JANITO GETS A DRAW.
Silvino Jumito met Paul Demsky in a twenty round contest at Brisbane, and the referee gave his decision as a draw.

label: paragraph_title
text: PRAISE NON PBLKY.

label: text
text:
'Solay Plexus,' writing in the Sydney Referee, has a good word for Young Pelky. He says: After watching his smashing methods against Bill Thurbon (who was knocked out in the tenth round). I aim confident that with an ounce of confidence and a little more polish to his boxing Tomario Pelky would be the most formidable lightweight seen in Australia for many day. Were he to make more use of his left in jabbing and shorten up his right he would be right there. In the gymnasium he is a champion, and it does not matter who his sparring partner may be. But the glare of the footlights and the crowd flurries him.
"Pelky is quick to learn anything shown him by his manager Baillieu and puts it into practice," but at this stage only in private. He is exceptionally tall; has no longer reach than most 9.9 men and can hit with the weight of many in good middleweight."

label: text
text: After a long and very successful career as lightweight champion of Australia, Sid Golfrey had to unclnowledge defeat at the hands of the tough and strong Harry Collins at the Sydney Stadium on April 11. A perfect right to the point put Golfrey down for the count in the tenth round.

label: text
text: The contest is described as the best seen in Sydney for a long time. With hanging on eliminated it was all fight, fast and furious, with victory to the fittest and best man. The man who had tried to win in every one of his hundred and more fights, and succeeded in 96. percent. of them, was forced to strike his colours to a more youthful and better conditioned opponent, who fought a better and more crafty fight than ever before.

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text:
ATTEMPT TO POPULARISE
GAME IN ENGLAND.

label: text
text: An Anglo-American Baseball Association has been formed in London, and the members are hopeful of popularising the game in England.

label: text
text: At present there are four teams proposed under the association—Chelsea, Brentford, London Lions, and American Legion.

label: text
text: The season opened on May 10, at Stamford Bridge Grounds, will in game between Chelsea and the s.s. Levinthan, followed on May 17 by Chelsea v. Oxford University. Other games to follow will be against the s.s. Pittsburgh, and a series against a picked team from the Paris Baseball League.

label: text
text: Mr. B. G. Gildersleeve, who managed the Chelsea side, did the pitching for that team, and Mr. Charles Brooks, who was out of the game last year owing to business obligations, is now managing the Brentford team, and will pitch for them.

label: text
text: Every possible assistance will be given to either clubs or individuals who wish to play, on communication with C. E. Bates, hon. secretary, care of Old Colony Club, Aldwych House, London, W.C.2.
